alternative: Initialise eagerly where it happens at load time (a file or require body runs once and require is serialised), or use concurrent-ruby (Concurrent::Delay for a one-shot promise, Concurrent::AtomicReference/Concurrent::Map for safe publication); if laziness is unavoidable, wrap the whole accessor in a Thread::Mutex#synchronize block and accept the cost instead of writing a double check.
idiom_name: Thread::Mutex-guarded accessor (no portable lock-free fast path exists)
implementation_notes: Ruby offers the classic form no cheap way to be sound: `@config ||= build` is check-then-act, the GVL that makes it look safe is a CRuby implementation detail, and neither JRuby nor TruffleRuby guarantees that a reference published by one thread is seen fully constructed by another; the only portable primitive is Thread::Mutex#synchronize, and putting the fast path inside the lock is the pattern with its entire benefit removed. The ecosystem answer is therefore structural: build the object at load time (a file or require body executes once and require is itself serialised), or use concurrent-ruby, whose Concurrent::Delay holds a one-shot promise that every reader waits on and Concurrent::AtomicReference gives volatile-style publication. Hand-written double-checked locking survives only as a legacy shape to recognise and refactor, not as a technique to introduce.
code_sketch:
# discouraged: there is no portable lock-free fast path in Ruby
DELAY = Concurrent::Delay.new { build_index }   # one-shot, thread-safe

def index
  DELAY.value                                   # waits on first call, cached after
end

# if laziness is unavoidable and concurrent-ruby is not an option:
# def index = (@mutex.synchronize { @index ||= build_index })
pitfalls: `@config ||= build` is not atomic: two threads can both build (duplicating side effects) and one result is discarded, and on non-CRuby implementations the publication itself is unordered.
The GVL hides the race on CRuby, so a green test suite proves nothing about the same code on JRuby or TruffleRuby - the bug appears only when the deployment changes.
Concurrent::Delay and Concurrent::Promise memoise failures: the exception is re-raised for every caller and the promise cannot be reset, so transient errors must be retried above it.
Class-level `@@var` accessors and eager class-body initialisation move the same shared state into load ordering, which fails differently (partially loaded constants) rather than safely.
